newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia well left alone by neighbours - Izetbegovic.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia well left alone by neighbours - Izetbegovic.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem leader Alija Izetbegovic said on Thursday that popular unrest in Serbia and Croatia would help to strengthen his country's independence.
"Both situations are creating a good environment so Bosnia Herzegovina can stand on its own feet," he told a news conference.
"Serbia will be preoccupied with itself for a long time and not with Bosnia-Herzegovina because of internal economic and social reasons."

Izetbegovic, chairman of Bosnia's three-member collective presidency, was referring to anti-government street protests in Serbia over the past six weeks and a demonstration in Croatia in support of an independent radio station.

He did not directly refer to reports that Croatian President Franjo Tudjman was seriously ill or that the ruling nationalist party was declining in popularity, but he predicted that democratic reforms were on the way in Croatia.
"Croatia's evolution into a democratic European state is an inevitable process. That was my assessment this summer and I am standing by that assessment," he said.
Bosnia's two powerful neighbours dominated the course of the war in former Yugoslavia and still control all its borders except for a small section in the southwest.
But Izetbegovic suggested that Croatia and Serbia would be less likely to interfere in Bosnia in future because of internal political disputes.
Referring to attempts by Serbian President Slobdoan Milosevic to crush street protests, he said: "I think those events will bring sobriety among the Serb people."
But the Serbian opposition needed to articulate its stance towards Bosnia, he added.

"As for the war in Bosnia they have said Milosevic is guilty but as for the position of the state and recognition of (Bosnia's) borders they have been silent so far and we are awaiting an answer," he said.
Izetbegovic said the past year had seen an end of war in Bosnia but important elements of a lasting peace had yet to materialise.
Refugees still were not being allowed to return to their homes, people still lacked free movement across former front lines and economic production still had to be revived, he said.
Izetbegovic said he expected a breakthrough in 1997 in the troubled Moslem-Croat federation, which together with a Serb republic comprises Bosnia.
He cited an agreement signed this month clearing the way for the formation of a joint Moslem-Croat police force as a major step forward.
"I have a feeling that this is the real thing, that this move will lead to the final establishment of the federation," he said.
The federation has existed primarily on paper since it was agreed two years ago under heavy pressure from the United States.
Moslems and Croats fought a bitter 10-month war for territory during the 1992-95 Bosnian conflict before renewing their alliance against separatist Serb forces.
